item.title: Pro-Palestine protesters rally in New York against Yoav Gallant
item.description: Pro-Palestinian demonstrators gathered in New York City on Wednesday, calling for the arrest of former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant and demanding that he leave the city, Anadolu reports. The protesters assembled at the corner of West 33rd Street and Seventh Avenue ahead of Gallant’s expected attendance at the opening of an annual summit organized by the pro-Israel Miriam Institute. Demonstrators cited an arrest warrant issued against Gallant by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2024, demanding that authorities take him into custody. item.title: Iran’s IRGC vows to challenge US blockade
item.description:
Iran’s IRGC vows to challenge US blockade

IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi says Tehran rejects a prolonged standoff with Washington and will act against the US blockade.

“We will not allow the continued naval, land, and air blockade imposed on our country,” he told Basij students in Tehran.

“We will not accept the continuation of the current status quo, a state of neither war nor peace, or a war of attrition.”

Mohebbi also made “resolving the issue of the Strait of Hormuz” a prerequisite for discussions on Iran’s nuclear programme.

item.title: How British sanctions are already having a material impact in the West Bank
item.description:
How British sanctions are already having a material impact in the West Bank

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Thu, 11/19/2026 - 12:37
Banks are freezing accounts of sanctioned Israeli companies even before the punitive measures have come into effect
Britain's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband at the G7 foreign ministers' summit at the Quai d'Orsay in Paris on 9 November (AFP)
Off

British sanctions targeting illegal Israeli settlements already appear to be having a material impact, even though most of the planned measures have yet to come into force.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the first set of sanctions on Tuesday. They targeted eight Israeli construction, property development and architectural businesses.

One of those firms is Har Hevron Development Company, which the British government said "carries out construction and infrastructure works for, and supplies housing units to, Israeli settlements and outposts in the southern West Bank".

On Thursday, Eliram Azulai, head of the Har Hevron Regional Council, told Israeli media that its foreign trade accounts have already been frozen by two banks. 

Azulai added that "this is only spreading further", saying he had heard other companies have had their services blocked.

On Wednesday, Hanan Friedman, the CEO of Israel's leading bank, Bank Leumi, announced that Israeli companies involved in West Bank settlement construction are struggling to receive financing from foreign banks, who are effectively imposing their own sanctions on the companies.

This emerging "credit freeze" has been widely linked in Israeli media to the sanctions announced by Britain, France and Canada in September. 

There is also some indication that the British sanctions have slowed down Israel's E1 settlement plan.

The Labour government’s timing in announcing its sanctions was in part motivated by a sense of urgency because of the plan, Middle East Eye understands. 

The E1 plan involves building thousands of new housing units between Jerusalem and the existing West Bank settlement of Maale Adumim, 7km east of the city. It would effectively cut the West Bank in half, making a Palestinian state unviable.

'Do not bid, do not build, and do not profit'

The first measures coming into force on Tuesday came shortly before E1 tenders were due to be allocated by the Israeli government. 

On Monday, Miliband said, "My message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution."

The following day, Gali Baharav-Miara, Israel's attorney general, ordered the Israeli government to postpone issuing the tenders. She said any decision on the E1 project should be taken by the new administration once it has formed.

Sources close to the British government insist the UK's measures played a role in impacting the decision, although Israeli diplomats have reportedly denied this.

But there is no doubt that the Israeli government is perturbed by the sanctions.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar described the new measures this week as a "hostile act targeting private, law-abiding companies".

He vowed retaliation, saying "Israel views with the utmost gravity the additional sanctions announced today", and promised to "respond to the British government’s actions with countermeasures. A wide range of possible responses is currently under consideration."

Amnesty International's UK arm praised the new measures as a "step in the right direction" but said they fall "far short of the action international law demands".

'Israel views with the utmost gravity the additional sanctions announced today'

 – Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar

Chris Doyle, the director of the Council for Arab-British Understanding, said: "This is a welcome first step under the new UK sanctions regime, including on construction companies but also Tsav, which blocks aid into Gaza."

But he argued the measures fail to address the role of the Israeli state itself in settlement expansion and restrictions on humanitarian aid entering Gaza.

Implementing the full sanctions announced in September could take up to nine months, according to government sources.

Senior UK government figures privately told MEE last month that even if Benjamin Netanyahu is no longer Israel's prime minister, they intend to implement comprehensive sanctions, including against companies providing construction and real estate services for settlement expansion.

But MEE understands that some officials have been pushing for the sanctions not to target British companies complicit in the illegal settlements, which would mean a watering down of the sanctions Miliband promised. 

As matters stand, however, the British measures already seem to be having something of an impact on the ground in the occupied territories.

item.title: Iraq avoids battle with powerful militia after 'compromise' reached to hand over stronghold
item.description:
Iraq avoids battle with powerful militia after 'compromise' reached to hand over stronghold

Submitted by Alex MacDonald on Thu, 11/19/2026 - 12:57
Iran-backed group Kataeb Hezbollah had earlier vowed not to evacuate Jurf al-Sakhar raising fears of clashes with Baghdad
Members of Iraq's Kataeb Hezbollah ride in the back of a pickup in their stronghold in Jurf al-Sakhar in Babil Province, south of Baghdad, on 17 November (AFP/Ahmad al-Rubaye)
Off

Baghdad has agreed a "compromise" with Kataeb Hezbollah over its Jurf al-Sakhar stronghold, narrowly avoiding outright conflict between the state and the Iran-backed militia.

The powerful paramilitary group had been given a deadline of Friday to hand over control of the area in southern Iraq, with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi readying security services near the outskirts, ready to enter by force.

Officials had accused Kataeb Hezbollah of running a smuggling ring from Jurf al-Sakhar that siphoned off hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil.

However, three senior security officials told Reuters on Thursday that a deal had been reached that would allow Baghdad authorities to enter the town on Friday.

Lieutenant General Saad Maan, head of Iraq's Security Media Cell, said the armed group's forces would move to other areas.

A new headquarters in Jurf al-Sakhar that reports to the federal police will go into operation at 6am on Friday, under the authority of the interior ministry.

It will be led by Lieutenant General Ahmed Hatem Hamid, alongside deputy commanders Major General Hussein Ali Nassif for defence affairs, and Adi Abdel-Imam Mussah for the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF).

The deal was brokered by senior Shia political leaders, with Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran's elite Quds Force, also arriving in Baghdad late on Monday to help defuse the situation.

'Even a limited clash around Jurf could have escalated quickly, especially if other factions saw it as the start of a broader move against them'

- Hayder al-Shakeri, analyst

As recently as Tuesday, Kataeb Hezbollah - whose well-armed and well-trained forces number in the tens of thousands by their own statements - had vowed they would not leave their stronghold.

"I can state decisively and with absolute certainty that the dream they dream of the Kataeb withdrawing from Jurf al-Sakhar will not come true, not even over our dead bodies," Abu Taleb al-Saidi, a Kataeb Hezbollah commander, told AFP during a press visit to the area.

Hayder al-Shakeri, a research fellow with the Middle East and North Africa programme at Chatham House, told Middle East Eye there were strong incentives for everyone to avoid conflict over Jurf al-Sakher.

"But the risk was still there if Zaidi kept pushing for a change on the ground while Kataeb Hezbollah refused to shift its position. In that scenario, even a limited clash around Jurf could have escalated quickly, especially if other factions saw it as the start of a broader move against them," he said.

"The deal mattered because it gave both sides a way to step back without either appearing to fully surrender."

State crackdown

On 29 September, the US announced the withdrawal of its forces from Iraq, 23 years after the invasion that overthrew Saddam Hussein.

The pullout was tied to the disarming of the extra-government armed groups that, since the overthrow of Saddam, have been among the most powerful forces in the country.

Most of them were formed in 2014 after a call from Shia religious leader Ali Sistani to mobilise and defend the country from the Islamic State (IS) group.

But the most powerful armed groups are older and, though they officially come under the authority of the state as part of Hashd al-Shaabi, or PMF, they are effectively independent and (for the most part) loyal to Iran.

Since Saddam's overthrow the groups have established control over much of Iraqi society, with deep links to the political establishment, military and organised crime.

As the US pulls its forces out of Iraq, what happens to Iran-backed armed groups?
Read More »

Zaidi said a deadline had been set for 30 June 2027 for the groups to disarm and/or come under direct state control.

But the most powerful of these groups - Kataeb Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba and Kataeb Sayyid al-Shuhada - have already said they are unwilling to do so.

During the US-led occupation and the war against IS, the groups were responsible for killing, kidnapping and torturing thousands of Iraqis, and helped suppress the pro-democracy Tishreen movement that erupted in 2019.

In recent years, a number of them have also grouped together under the heading of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq to target Israeli and US assets over the ongoing genocide in Gaza.

Hisham al-Mozani, an activist with Al-Amal Association rights group, told Middle East Eye in September that the push to disarm the groups risked returning the country to civil war.

"For the army and security forces, maybe they will have clashes with the militias and that's a very, very dangerous thing - it will affect the economy, affect security in all of Iraq," he said.

He said he believed the process of disarming and integrating the groups would take around five years, even if the process began at all.

"Some of these militias are more than 40 years old, since the Iran-Iraq war in 1980, so they've had a long time and they're in the political parties, are present in the parliament and some of them are in the ministries," he said.

UK: Activist scales Spanish embassy in London in protest over Fergie Chambers case
item.description:
UK: Activist scales Spanish embassy in London in protest over Fergie Chambers case

Submitted by Areeb Ullah on Thu, 11/19/2026 - 13:08
Healthcare worker stages five-hour rooftop protest demanding Madrid halt extradition proceedings against Chambers
Welsh healthcare worker Leigh Evans occupying the roof of the Spanish embassy in London to oppose the extradition of Fergie Chambers from Spain to the United States (screenshot)
Off

A Welsh healthcare worker who sailed on a Gaza aid flotilla has been arrested after climbing onto the roof of the Spanish embassy in London to protest the ongoing extradition proceedings in Madrid against pro-Palestinian activist Fergie Chambers.

Wearing blue scrubs and a black-and-white keffiyeh, Leigh Evans scaled the embassy building in central London in the early hours of Thursday morning.

Evans then began reading out a speech calling on Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to grant Chambers political asylum and halt his potential extradition to the United States.

He spent five hours on the roof, closing the embassy to the public, before police were called to arrest him.

Photos of the scene showed Evans being brought down by police officers and firefighters on the platform of a fire engine.

In a statement issued before his arrest, Evans accused the Spanish government of enabling Washington's "political persecution" of Chambers over his financial backing of pro-Palestine causes.

"Fergie Chambers is being imprisoned in Spain at the behest of Trump because he is one of the largest humanitarian donors to Gaza," Evans said in the statement.

"Fergie is the first political prisoner in Spanish history imprisoned over his support for Palestine. Every day that he is in prison brings further shame on Prime Minister Sanchez."

Evans is a veteran campaigner who has protested for Gaza and the rights of the Palestinian people.

Last year, Evans took part in a flotilla attempting to open a humanitarian corridor to Gaza, where he was intercepted at sea and held by Israeli forces before being released in October 2025.

He was also arrested outside the Welsh Parliament, or Senedd, last year for protesting against the British government's proscription of Palestine Action.

Chambers denies charges

Chambers, an heir to the Cox family fortune, was arrested on the Spanish island of Ibiza in July following a US extradition request.

If extradited and convicted on the lead charge of international money laundering, Chambers could face a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.

'Every day that [Chambers] is in prison brings further shame on Prime Minister Sanchez'

- Leigh Evans, pro-Palestine activist

Last Friday, Chambers appeared publicly for the first time since his arrest in Spain and told a Spanish court that he supported relief efforts in Gaza because Israel's genocidal war in the Palestinian territory had become “the prevailing moral question of our time”.

In September, the Spanish government came under fire for allowing the case to proceed to the courts after declining to block the US request at the preliminary stage.

The court is expected to deliver its decision imminently, with the Spanish government also having a role in the extradition process.

According to the indictment, US prosecutors charged Chambers with international money laundering, riot and conspiracy to riot. They allege that, after leaving the United States in 2023, he transferred approximately $7.5m out of the country with the intent of providing material support to Hamas.

Chambers disputed the allegations, maintaining that the funds were used for lawful purposes, including investments in local businesses and sponsorship of a football team in Tunisia.

He also insisted his involvement in protest actions was non-violent.

The activist also addressed allegations in the US indictment concerning large financial transfers to Club Africain, the reigning Tunisian football champions, who won their first league title in 11 years in May.

He said he was introduced to the club soon after relocating to Tunis and quickly became a supporter.

After discovering that the club was deeply in debt and struggling to fulfil its contracts and pay staff, Chambers said he negotiated a sponsorship agreement between Club Africain and a sports company he had established in the city.

The agreement was worth four million euros over four years, he said, with additional funding intended to eliminate debts, rehabilitate the club’s youth programme and settle years of unpaid salaries in its women’s sections.

Asked about his involvement with Palestine Action USA, Chambers described the group as less an organisation than “an idea of protest”, particularly against Elbit Systems, Israel’s largest arms manufacturer.
